repairs.value: Carrier argues that Josephus, Philo, Essene parallels, and several Pauline passages distinguish earthly from heavenly bodies, making Paul’s body-exchange interpretation textually and historically more plausible.

Strongest feature: Carrier widens his case beyond the disputed vocabulary of 1 Corinthians 15 by aligning Josephus, Philo, Essene thought, Philippians, and 2 Corinthians with a coherent replacement-body reading. Principal limitation: Those parallels establish an interpretive possibility rather than Paul’s adoption of it; Carrier later answers Licona on Romans’ present-life context and the exchange verb, yet Licona’s reincarnation distinction and transformation reading keep the inference contested. Live burden: The exchange reading must show why its clothing, dwelling, decay, and heavenly-citizenship language controls Paul’s bodily continuity claims more decisively than Licona’s predicates concerning mortal and lowly bodies. Locked score: The fixed score of 83 rewards Carrier’s source-linked rebuttal and its genuine scholarly plausibility while withholding stronger credit because the crucial inference from comparative resemblance to Paul’s own intended ontology remains contested.

contextualSupport.reason: Licona distinguishes reincarnation from resurrection and argues Romans and Philippians support transformation.
Carrier later answers the Romans context, exchange verb, continuity grammar, and mortality idiom.
